strengths: Timely and well-motivated task: While controllable generation (e.g., ControlNet) is mature for image and video synthesis, extending unified control (both visual structure/identity and acoustic timbre) to native joint audio-video Diffusion Transformers (such as LTX-2) addresses an important gap in multimodal generation.

Well-designed and non-intrusive architecture: The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides a clean interface for tokenizing heterogeneous controls (reference image, reference audio, structural sequences) using channel and temporal masking. The Dual-Stream Bypass architecture preserves pre-trained foundation priors by keeping the joint backbone frozen and injecting contextual hints via zero-initialized gated residuals.

Decoupled inference control: The introduction of Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling allows users to independently adjust visual and acoustic guidance strengths at inference time without retraining, offering clear practical utility for creative workflows.

Solid empirical evaluation: The paper conducts comprehensive evaluations across multiple settings—audio-driven talking generation, depth control, and pose control—supplemented by thorough audio quality metrics (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER), a user study, and ablation studies examining bypass components and guidance scales.
weaknesses: Dataset and domain diversity: The model is trained on a 30k subset of the Hallo3 dataset, which consists primarily of portrait and upper-body talking human videos. Consequently, nearly all qualitative examples and benchmarks focus on single-speaker talking heads. The paper does not thoroughly explore how well the framework generalizes to open-domain joint audio-video generation (e.g., complex multi-agent scenes, natural landscapes, ambient environmental sounds, or non-speech acoustics).

Incremental architectural novelty: The core building blocks heavily draw upon well-established conditioning paradigms (ControlNet bypass branches, adapter-style feature injection, and temporal latent concatenation). The primary novelty lies in synthesizing these mechanisms into a joint audio-video DiT framework rather than fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs.

Baseline fairness and attribution: Many baselines (e.g., SadTalker, Text2Video-Zero, ControlVideo) rely on significantly smaller, older foundational backbones compared to the powerful 19B LTX-2 foundation model used by MMControl. It is somewhat difficult to isolate how much of the performance advantage stems from the proposed MMCU/Dual-Stream mechanism versus the underlying capacity of the frozen LTX-2 19B backbone.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: extending controllable generation to native joint audio-video diffusion transformers (DiTs), an area currently under-explored compared to visual-only controllable video models.

Well-structured framework design: the Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides an elegant masking and token concatenation mechanism to handle heterogeneous visual, acoustic, and structural conditions within a single unified interface.
The Dual-Stream Bypass architecture enables non-intrusive injection into frozen joint DiT blocks, preserving foundation model priors while remaining parameter-efficient and stable to train.

Modality-specific guidance scaling ($\gamma_v, \gamma_a$) offers valuable inference-time flexibility, allowing users to independently balance visual structure and audio/timbre fidelity without retraining.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse tasks (reference-based audio-video generation, depth control, and pose control), supported by standard quantitative metrics (VBench, Sync-C/D, MAE, UTMOS, WER) as well as human perceptual studies and thorough ablation experiments in the appendix.
weaknesses: The training and evaluation data are primarily derived from Hallo3 (30,000 samples), which consists largely of human-centric/talking-face videos. The paper would benefit from discussing the generalization limits to open-domain multi-modal generation (e.g., non-human scenes, ambient environmental sounds, multi-speaker conversational settings).

Clarification is needed regarding the combination of structural signals: Eq. (2) defines $S$ as either depth or pose sequences. It is unclear whether the current MMCU framework can simultaneously condition on multiple concurrent structural inputs (e.g., pose AND depth simultaneously), or if each structural condition must be trained/injected separately.

In Table 1, baseline methods (SadTalker, AniPortrait, Hallo3) are conditioned on ground-truth audio while MMControl generates audio from text. While the authors note this distinction, more detail regarding prompt harmonization and reference frame selection across all baselines would ensure fully transparent comparability.

Being a multimodal audio-video paper, visual figures in print cannot fully showcase temporal coherence, lip-synchronization precision, and acoustic timbre quality; including supplementary video/audio samples or demo recordings is essential for comprehensive perceptual verification.

strengths: Timely and relevant focus: While joint audio-video foundation models (such as LTX-2) have advanced rapidly, fine-grained multi-modal control combining structural visual priors (depth, pose) and reference acoustic/visual identity within a unified joint DiT framework remains under-explored.

Well-structured framework: The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides a clean interface for handling heterogeneous control conditions via temporal concatenation and binary masks, and the Dual-Stream Bypass enables non-intrusive injection into frozen joint DiT blocks without disrupting pre-trained priors.

Decoupled test-time control: Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling allows independent tuning of visual structural adherence and acoustic timbre fidelity at inference time, offering practical user control without retraining.

Thorough evaluation and ablations: The experimental section and appendix provide quantitative visual metrics, audio-visual synchronization metrics (Sync-C/D), acoustic metrics (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER), human evaluation, and comprehensive component ablations validating the architectural choices.
weaknesses: Fairness and capacity gap in baseline comparisons: The comparisons across tasks pit MMControl (built upon the large 19B LTX-2 DiT backbone) against significantly smaller or older models (e.g., VideoComposer, Text2Video-Zero, SadTalker). As a result, improvements in visual aesthetics, DINO subject similarity, and motion smoothness may largely stem from the base generative model capacity rather than the proposed control mechanism alone.

Limited acoustic control scope: Although framed as unified multi-modal control, the acoustic conditioning is largely confined to voice timbre matching via reference audio embeddings and silence placeholders for target speech generation, without extending to more granular acoustic controls (such as pitch contours, audio events, or ambient acoustic guidance).

Dataset scale and domain diversity: The model is trained on a 30,000-clip subset derived from Hallo3, which predominantly comprises talking-head and portrait sequences. It remains unclear how robustly the depth and pose guidance generalize to complex open-domain scenes, fast camera trajectories, or multiple interacting subjects.

Architectural novelty is relatively incremental: The dual-stream bypass and temporal concatenation of reference latents are largely natural adaptations of well-established conditioning paradigms (such as ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, and inpainting/continuation framing) to a dual-stream joint DiT backbone.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: As generative modeling shifts towards native joint audio-video Diffusion Transformers (e.g., LTX-2), fine-grained multi-modal control that spans both visual (identity, depth, pose) and acoustic (timbre) modalities is an important and under-explored topic.

Clean and modular system design: The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) elegantly unifies heterogeneous temporal control signals and reference tokens with mask channels, while the Dual-Stream Bypass enables effective condition injection into frozen joint DiT backbones without disrupting pre-trained priors.

Flexible inference control: The introduction of Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling allows practitioners to independently tune the guidance strengths of visual identity, structural layout, and voice timbre.

Extensive evaluation across modalities: The paper evaluates structural alignment (MAE), video quality and identity (CLIP, Subject DINO, VBench), audio-visual synchronization (Sync-C, Sync-D), speech quality (UTMOS, SIM-o, WER), and human perceptual quality.
weaknesses: Domain scope restricted to talking humans: The training dataset (30,000 samples from Hallo3) and all evaluated benchmarks are strictly centered around talking humans and portrait videos. The paper's framing suggests general joint audio-video generation, but open-domain general audio-visual scenarios (e.g., non-human scenes, animal sounds, foley effects with action control) are neither evaluated nor discussed.

Lack of systematic quantitative ablations: While qualitative results are shown for guidance scaling in Figure 7, the paper lacks quantitative ablation studies isolating critical architectural choices—such as the impact of the mask channel projection, interleaved even-layer placement versus alternative bypass configurations, or quantitative tradeoffs across different values of $\gamma_v$ and $\gamma_a$.

Baseline comparability constraints: Because prior works are largely divided into either video-only structural control (e.g., VACE, VideoComposer) or audio-driven talking head synthesis (e.g., SadTalker, Hallo3), the comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 operate under asymmetric conditioning settings. Comparing against straightforward adapters (e.g., ControlNet-style visual injection) directly on the base LTX-2 model would provide a more direct point of comparison.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: As generative modeling shifts towards native joint audio-video diffusion transformers (DiTs), introducing fine-grained, multi-modal controllable generation (covering visual structure, visual identity, and voice timbre simultaneously) addresses an important emerging challenge.

Well-structured framework: The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides a clean, unified temporal concatenation and masking representation for heterogeneous signals, while the Dual-Stream Bypass preserves pre-trained generative priors without intrusive modification to the backbone.

Practical inference flexibility: The Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling allows users to independently navigate trade-offs between structural/identity adherence and generative freedom across the audio and video streams at test time.

Promising qualitative and human evaluation results: The generated videos show consistent identity, synchronized lip motions, and faithful structural alignment (depth/pose), supported by a comprehensive 6-criterion user study.
weaknesses: Discrepancy between general claims and domain scope: The manuscript frames the contribution as general 'Multi-Modal Controllable Joint Audio-Video Generation', yet the training data (curated 30k subset from Hallo3) and all experimental evaluations/figures are restricted exclusively to talking human portraits. The authors should either clearly scope their claims to human/portrait generation or demonstrate generalization to broader audio-visual scenes (e.g., ambient sound, actions, musical instruments).

Lack of quantitative ablation studies: There are no systematic quantitative ablations evaluating core architectural decisions, such as: (1) interleaving bypass blocks every two layers vs. every layer; (2) removing audio-to-video / video-to-audio cross-attention in the bypass; (3) impact of the MMCU mask channel projection; and (4) quantitative sensitivity curves for the guidance scales $\gamma_v$ and $\gamma_a$.

Missing baseline context in audio evaluation: While Table S2 provides audio metrics (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER), there are no comparative baseline numbers (e.g., base LTX-2, dedicated zero-shot TTS models like ZipVoice/Seed-TTS, or cascaded baselines) to establish whether an average WER of 17.58% or SIM-o of 0.2574 represents strong or mediocre performance in this setting.

Asymmetry in baseline comparisons: In Table 1, comparing a joint text-to-audio-video model with image-and-audio-driven portrait animation methods (SadTalker, AniPortrait, Hallo3) that receive ground-truth audio makes direct metric comparison slightly uneven. A comparison against base LTX-2 (with prompt conditioning) or other joint AV foundations would better isolate the exact gains of the proposed control adapters.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely task: extending controllable generation paradigms (identity, structure, timbre) to joint audio-video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs).
The proposed Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides a clean, unified tokenization and masking formulation for heterogeneous visual and acoustic conditions.

The dual-stream bypass design allows training control signals without altering pre-trained backbone weights, while modality-specific guidance scaling provides flexible inference-time steering between modalities.
Promising qualitative results demonstrating simultaneous control over character identity, speech timbre, and geometric guidance (depth/pose).
weaknesses: Limited dataset domain despite general claims: The model is trained exclusively on 30,000 samples from Hallo3, which is fundamentally a talking-head/portrait dataset. Consequently, the claim of general multi-modal controllable joint video generation is overstated, as the experiments are essentially restricted to upper-body talking humans.

Mismatched baseline comparisons: In Table 1, MMControl is compared against portrait animation models (SadTalker, AniPortrait, Hallo3) that take ground-truth driving audio rather than text. Meanwhile, Table S2 evaluates audio quality (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER) purely in isolation without comparing against any competitive cascaded TTS + video pipelines or audio-video foundation baselines.

Lack of quantitative ablations: The manuscript does not provide quantitative ablation studies to validate core architectural choices, such as the effectiveness of the dual-stream bypass versus LoRA/adapter alternatives, bypass layer placement, the necessity of the MMCU masking scheme, or quantitative sensitivity to guidance scales (gamma_v, gamma_a).

Incomplete structural evaluation: While depth control is evaluated quantitatively via MAE in Table 2, pose-conditioned generation is evaluated only through a single qualitative figure (Figure 6) without standard quantitative metrics (e.g., PCK or keypoint error).

Limited architectural novelty: The dual-stream bypass mechanism is largely a direct adaptation of existing ControlNet/T2I-Adapter paradigms to the two-stream structure of the pre-trained LTX-2 backbone.
